title: Jharkhand exam protests in Ranchi: After CJP, a new youth agitation grips Indian state
description: Image source, Sartaj AlamImage caption, Dozens of students and job aspirants are on a hunger strike in Ranchi ByZoya MateenReporting fromDelhi and Moh
body: Image source, Sartaj AlamImage caption, Dozens of students and job aspirants are on a hunger strike in Ranchi ByZoya MateenReporting fromDelhi and Mohammad Sartaj AlamReporting fromRanchi, JharkhandWeeks after thousands of young Indians poured onto the streets of Delhi in a major 'cockroach' protest over examination paper leaks, another group of frustrated job seekers is making headlines - this time hundreds of miles away, in the eastern state of Jharkhand.Protesters have gathered at a stadium in the state capital Ranchi, since 25 July, demanding an overhaul of the state's government examination system. Some have been sleeping in the open and several have gone on hunger strike.Umme Habiba is one of them.The 27-year-old, from a farming family from Bokaro, has spent years preparing for Jharkhand's civil service examination, hoping it would get her the security of a government job. She has already sat the exam three times and hoped to get a good score this time."We want justice. We will not leave until we get it, even if it costs us our lives," she said.The immediate cause of the anger is a preliminary civil service examination held in April. After the results were announced in July, candidates alleged that leaked answer sheets shared on social media showed some successful applicants had answered far fewer questions than expected. This fuelled suspicions that the results had been manipulated. The protesters want the exam scrapped and held again. They also want the case investigated by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's premier federal investigative agency.The allegations are being investigated by Jharkhand's Criminal Investigation Department (CID) and the Jharkhand Public Service Commission has since postponed the next stage of the examination. Its chairman, L Khiangte, resigned on 22 July and has been questioned as part of the investigation.Investigators are also examining the role of a private company that conducted parts of the examination process, after candidates raised questions about how it was selected.Deepika Pandey Singh, a minister in the Jharkhand government, told the BBC that the state had begun investigating the allegations even before the current protest.She urged protesters to let the CID complete its investigation instead of handing the case to the CBI. "We want a fair investigation," she said, adding that anyone responsible - "whether a bureaucrat, employee, middleman or a big politician" - would face action. She also said the government would discuss the protesters' demand to cancel the April exam with them directly.Image source, Sartaj AlamImage caption, Umme Habiba says young people in Jharkhand are fed up with the discrepancies in the state's examination system But protesters say their fight goes beyond one exam. They want a wider probe into alleged recruitment irregularities, action against those responsible and long-delayed hiring completed on time. Above all, they want regular, transparent exams so candidates are no longer left waiting indefinitely.The stakes are especially high in India, where a government job offers a steady salary, social status and a route into the middle class. Competition is fierce, and many candidates spend years chasing one.In Jharkhand, protesters say the uncertainty only prolongs the wait. As friends find jobs, marry and move on, many remain dependent on their parents. With every delayed exam, stalled recruitment and fresh controversy, the future they have worked towards slips further away.For Savita Kumari, the wait began in 2019. Now 28, she has taken the state civil service exam twice. Confident she had cleared this year's preliminary stage, she stayed up for the results, released around midnight. Her name was missing. "We cried the whole night," she said.Savita believes the exam was manipulated, alleging some candidates left answers blank so they could be filled in later. The CID has since sought answer sheets from successful candidates and raided the offices of the Jharkhand Public Service Commission and other locations.Image source, Sartaj AlamImage caption, Protesters have been pouring in since 25 July - and have refused to leave That loss of faith is not confined to Jharkhand. Last month, the much larger protests in Delhi became one of the sharpest expressions of youth anger over examinations and jobs in recent years. The Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, the independent youth movement behind those demonstrations, has since announced its support for the protests in Jharkhand.There are other echoes of Delhi in Ranchi, too. Nearly two weeks into the protest, the camp has settled into a routine. Supporters bring food, water and supplies, some through CJP networks. During the day, hunger strikers lie on mattresses under tarpaulins, with portraits of BR Ambedkar and freedom fighters behind them. Even monsoon rain does little to empty the camp.By evening, the mood shifts. Crowds swell, speeches begin and slogans echo across the stadium. For a few hours, the encampment comes alive again.There is one key difference. Unlike the CJP protests, which emerged outside party politics, the Ranchi agitation has drawn strong political backing.The BJP, which is in opposition in Jharkhand, has backed the protesters, staged demonstrations, raised the issue in the state assembly and demanded a federal investigation. Congress, a partner in the state government but the BJP's national rival, has also expressed support for the students.Image source, Sartaj AlamImage caption, Devendra Nath Mahto is widely seen as the face of the protests One of the protest's most visible faces is Devendra Nath Mahto, who is also on hunger strike. A former state election candidate, he says he began campaigning over recruitment issues while still a student. In 2023, he joined protests over another state examination despite not having taken the test himself."Even if I didn't take the exam today," he said, "I will have to take it tomorrow."Many protesters are wary of being claimed by any political party and insist that the movement remains theirs."Students will lead this movement," said Vikram Kumar. "They will be on the stage and in front." Politicians are welcome to support them, he said, but should "leave their party's flag and agenda at home".Kumar has been waiting since 2019 for the state to recruit assistant engineers. He said the examination has been advertised only three times since Jharkhand state was created in 2000, even as hundreds of posts remain vacant. "All we get is assurances," he said. The government has offered talks, and the protesters have formed an 11-member delegation, though the two sides were yet to meet formally by Friday. Habiba remains wary. She says the protesters have heard promises before; what they want now is an investigation they trust and examinations they believe are fair.For now, they are still waiting.

schema.headline: Jharkhand exam protests in Ranchi: After CJP, a new youth agitation grips Indian state

title: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence agreement
description: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an attack on one of them would be seen as an attack on all three.The p
body: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have signed a joint defence agreement, saying an attack on one of them would be seen as an attack on all three.The pact was announced at a meeting between Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in the Saudi city of Mecca.After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Tehran and its allies struck targets in Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a major oil shipping channel, and the Red Sea.The Mecca agreement has drawn a sharp reaction from Tehran, where an senior member of parliament said it would not help Saudi Arabia."The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan does not bring them security, just as years of unilateral milking of the Americans did not bring them security," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of National Security commission, wrote on his X.Saudi Arabia and Pakistan had already announced a joint defence pact last year.The new Mecca Joint Defence Agreement sees three of the world's most powerful Muslim nations come together to offer mutual defence guarantees.It aims "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all", a joint statement reads."It further provides for the enhancement of all aspects of defence co-operation among the three States."Although the pact pledges mutual support, it provides no specifics on the obligations of each party. A Turkish official quoted by Reuters news agency said the pact was "purely defensive in nature".Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey each bring different qualities to the table, with each wanting something different out of it.For the Saudis, this gives an extra level of security in a region whose security architecture has been upended by the US and Israel's war with Iran.Last month, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels – who control much of the north-west of the country - announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and targeted Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.Furthermore, the Saudis will be keenly aware of last year's Israeli strikes on Doha, targeting senior Hamas officials. According to a report last year by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, external, "across the Gulf, states recalibrated their defence strategies". This pact is one of Saudi Arabia's responses.For Pakistan, the pact offers different but complementary benefits. In May 2025 its long-standing tensions with India boiled over into open conflict.While an all-out war was avoided, having the economic muscle of Saudi Arabia and the military and industrial might of Turkey in their corner will be seen as increasingly valuable.It also comes at a time when Pakistan has been taking on a far more significant role in global diplomacy. It has acted as an intermediary between Iran and the US and hosted ceasefire negotiations, significantly increasing its status in the region - something this pact further cements.As for Turkey, the benefits are different. According to Burcu Ozcelik from the London-based Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), the deal offers opportunities for the country's significant defence industries through "joint production, technology partnerships, procurement and greater military interoperability".While, on the surface, the concept of a mutual defence agreement seems straightforward, in practice the circumstances in which they would come into play are both complex and uncertain.Would, for example, Turkey be obliged to join in strikes on Yemen if Saudi Arabia's full-scale war with the Houthis were to restart?Would Saudi Arabia have to declare war on India were there to be a re-emergence of conflict with Pakistan?Each instance would require complex calculations and careful diplomacy, often in an attempt to avoid escalation. It is, in short, uncertain.The one consequence of a mutual defence agreement that sides involved will be banking on, however, is deterrence.The very fact that they each now have two other regional powers standing behind them may not make aggression impossible, but it will make its potential cost significantly higher.

schema.headline: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan sign defence agreement

title: Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds
description: Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supportin
body: Some estimates made by Doge, the body charged with reducing US government spending, that it saved billions of dollars are "incorrect or lack supporting evidence", a watchdog has found. A report released on Thursday by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has given an extensive review of Doge's claims about its so-called "Wall of Receipts", which reported savings of $110bn (£82bn) across contracts, grants and leases."Several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the report stated.Asked for comment, a White House official said the administration told the GAO that all employees had to complete ethics training and follow financial disclosure requirements.Doge, the Department of Government Efficiency, was not an official government department. It launched at the start of President Trump's second term but closed last month. Its Wall of Receipts was a way of showing its purported savings in taxpayer money online. Elon Musk, the billionaire boss of Tesla and SpaceX who formerly led Doge but left in May 2025, initially promised to save as much as $2tn a year by slashing federal jobs and shuttering government programmes, among other cost-cutting measures. Even by Doge's own estimates, it fell short of that goal, as its website claims to have saved an estimated $214bn."While Doge provided some information about estimated savings, several issues limit the transparency and reliability of these reported savings," the GAO report stated.It said Doge had not been transparent regarding the methods it used to calculate savings, highlighting it "did not provide sufficient information to verify the method used to calculate 96% of Doge-reported savings". Among its specific findings was that 108 of the 264 leases identified by Doge for termination were already in the process of ending before the body was established.That accounts for about $15.3m of the total $53.5m in savings Doge claimed."The Wall of Receipts does not include an explanation of how the savings from terminated leases were calculated," the GAO said.Claims were also made about savings that were not achieved, like $1.7bn for ending a defence department contract for IT services. However, the contract was never terminated and thus no savings were achieved, according to the congressional watchdog's report."While the Wall of Receipts includes some information about the data and sources underlying reported savings, it does not sufficiently disclose limitations affecting data quality," it assessed.The GAO audit, which was carried out at the request of Democratic Senators Gary Peters and Richard Blumenthal, covered savings data reported from 20 January  2025 through 7 July 2026."Everyone supports rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, but Doge was a slapdash and deceptive effort that misled the American people while doing real damage to the government's ability to serve them," Senator Peters said in a statement on Thursday.Under Musk, Doge pushed for massive reductions in the federal workforce, as well as the shuttering of programmes and even agencies such as the US Agency for International Development (USAID).Some of Doge's moves were met with legal fights, or were reversed. When the group's cost-cutting resulted in bird flu officials at the US Department of Agriculture being fired, the Trump administration looked to re-hire them days later.In a social media post last month announcing its closure, Doge said: "While the formal mission of Doge has come to an end, the mission to eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse will continue. Good stewardship of taxpayer dollars and accountable government are not temporary initiatives."

schema.headline: Doge overstated claims to have saved Americans $110bn, watchdog finds

title: Australian aviation crew carries out daring midwinter Antarctica rescue
description: An Australian aviation crew has carried out a daring midwinter mission to rescue a US expedition member from a station in Antarctica in freezing tempe
body: An Australian aviation crew has carried out a daring midwinter mission to rescue a US expedition member from a station in Antarctica in freezing temperatures and total darkness.Skytraders said the "extraordinary" mission took place last Friday after a request for urgent help with a medical evacuation from McMurdo Station.After an initial delay due to the weather, the aviation company said it was able to land its Airbus A319 in "extremely challenging conditions" including temperatures of -43C (-45.4F).The patient was then safely transferred onto the plane, known as Snowbird 1, which carried on to Christchurch in New Zealand, where the patient was treated. He is now recovering well.Captain Louise Robertson, one of four pilots on the flight which took off from the Tasmanian city of Hobart, told the BBC it was the first ever to have taken place in July and to be completed in total darkness."We completed it on the 31 July, and the first day of any sort of sunlight, which was very minimal, would be on the 1 August," she said.Her husband of 18 years, Rod Robertson, was the pilot who landed the plane at the US research station on Ross Island. "He was in the left seat and I was in the right seat," she said, adding that it was the most complex operation she had ever been involved in during her seven years at Skytraders and 25 as a pilot.Skytraders had received the evacuation request from the US Antarctic Program via the Australian Antarctic Division on Wednesday afternoon, Robertson said. It was a "major operation" for the plane to be correctly configured in time by engineers and a design team, who fitted a stretcher in the back.The configuration took 24 hours, Robertson said, but takeoff was then delayed for another 12 hours while the crew waited for a suitable window in the weather.  "We had quite a narrow time frame that we could actually fly down to Antarctica because there was a snowstorm on the first day that we were intending to go down which stopped the operation."The storm prevented crew at the station from getting to the runway, made of compacted snow, which had to be graded and groomed to make it smooth - a six-hour job.The plane eventually took off from Hobart in the early hours of Friday morning.The ground crew "did a phenomenal job to make a 3-km-long runway available for us given the conditions they were also facing, -45C and strong wind," Robertson said.The flight crew spent exactly one hour on the ground at Phoenix Airfield before taking off again for Christchurch.Another pilot on the mission, Captain Al Wallach, said the success reflected the specialist expertise of the team, which included the flight crews, meteorologists, operational planners, runway teams and medical personnel. "Every Antarctic mission demands absolute precision, but winter operations raise the complexity significantly," he said. "The conditions we encountered were right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability."Emma Campbell, head of the Australian Antarctic Division, said the operation "highlights both the capability of our people and the strong partnerships that underpin Antarctic programmes around the world".Skytraders carried out a similar mission in March 2020, when the US requested help evacuating a member of the US Antarctic Program also based in McMurdo, although temperatures were slightly warmer at -30°C.

schema.headline: Australian aviation crew carries out daring midwinter Antarctica rescue

title: Trump administration to pay German firm to halt US wind projects
description: RWE said it has agreed to relinquish its leases off the California and Louisiana coasts as well as in the New York Bight.Overall, the German firm plan
body: RWE said it has agreed to relinquish its leases off the California and Louisiana coasts as well as in the New York Bight.Overall, the German firm plans to invest approximately €17bn (£14.5bn; $19.6bn) in the US over the next six years "to grow its generation capacity".Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said in a statement posted on X that Americans deserve an energy system built on common sense and not one dependent on "costly subsidies". "We welcome RWE's agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation's energy security," he added.The deal is the latest the Trump administration has reached this year as Trump, a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry, continues his push to halt offshore wind projects.Trump has sought to boost government support for fossil fuels after campaigning for the presidency under the slogan "drill, baby, drill".Days after his return to office, he said "we're not going to do the wind thing" and called them "big, ugly windmills" that were dangerous to wildlife.And this week, he said that "any country with windmills is a loser".In March 2026, the DoI reached a deal with TotalEnergies putting an end to the French company's offshore wind projects in the US.Instead, the firm agreed to reroute investment to build a LNG plant in Texas and to develop "upstream conventional oil" in the Gulf of Mexico.The administration signed a similar $129m (£96m) agreement with Charlotte-based Duke Energy last month in exchange for the termination of the company's offshore wind lease in the Carolina Long Bay area.

schema.headline: Trump administration to pay German firm to halt US wind projects

title: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies
description: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started
body: Spain has imposed border controls on all air and sea travel from Italy as a row between the two EU countries intensifies.The measures - which started at midnight (22:00 GMT) and will last for a month - come a week after Italy introduced similar restrictions following an influx of about 78,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.On Friday, Spain demanded Italy reverse its checks by Sunday. Rome said they would stay until at least 15 August - when, it said, Spain "expects a new wave of migration" to hit Ceuta.The crisis has pitted Spain's socialist leader Pedro Sanchez against Italy's conservative leader Giorgia Meloni - who has long called for stricter EU migration rules.Italy does not share a land border with Spain. Its government said last week that decision to temporarily suspend the ​border-free Schengen arrangement was to prevent any of the migrants who had entered Ceuta from travelling on to Italy.Madrid dismissed this position, saying it was based on "spurious arguments" that lacked any basis in fact because the migrants who entered Ceuta had no way of entering the Schengen area. In its response to the Spanish threat earlier on Friday, Italy's government said it would not accept "ultimatums". It added that it did not intend "under any circumstances to reconsider the decision to suspend the application of the Schengen Agreement for third-country nationals arriving from Spain, at least until August 15th and in any case until security and terrorist risks for Italy have been completely eliminated".Italian officials have said local authorities carrying out checks do "everything possible" to ensure maximum comfort for both Spanish and other European citizens arriving in Italy from Spain.Rome has also reiterated that Spanish citizens are exempt from additional checks when arriving in Italy, with these extra steps only for non-EU residents.However, El Pais reported that several airport terminals have seen long queues and waiting times in recent days, with passengers arriving from Spain directed to a specific line for checks.The counter-measures Madrid decided to impose on Friday would include passport, nationality and visa checks for Italian passengers and visitors from other countries arriving from Italy "amid the persistent irregular migratory pressure" the country was experiencing, a statement from Spain's government said.Checks would stay in place until 7 September "unless a change in the circumstances that led to its adoption warrants modifying that period".

schema.headline: Spain to impose border controls against Italy as row over Ceuta migrant influx intensifies

title: Trump again limits US birthright citizenship with new executive orders
description: Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate
body: Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate the right.The president signed two executive orders on Thursday, including one that expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.The second order bans so-called birth tourism, the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies will be citizens. "This should have happened years ago, but we're taking care of it now," Trump said from the Oval Office, criticising the Supreme Court's rejection of his previous bid to end the 150-year-old policy. "My Administration has guarded against the risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation," the first executive order says.That order prohibits the automatic citizenship of babies born in the United States to two non-citizen parents where one of the parents is: a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.Birthright citizenship for people born in US territories such as Puerto Rico is codified by federal statute. Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly railed against birth tourism, including accusing Russian and Chinese adversaries of taking advantage of birthright citizenship to infiltrate the US. While announcing the executive orders from the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump said that hundreds of thousands of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US. The Migration Policy Institute, a nonpartisan research group, has said that the most expansive census-based estimate accounts for about 22,000 to 26,000 babies born in the US from birth tourism every year. Government data, according to the institute, showed that there were 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024."The idea (is) that people come here pretending to be a tourist, pretending to be a visitor," Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said while standing beside the president on Thursday."But the real reason they're here is to have a child, to make that child an automatic citizen, (to) leave our country and then have a US citizen child," he said, adding that those children then gain access to welfare benefits, the voting booth, and "all the other rights and privileges that belong solely to Americans".Miller said the president has the authority to ban birth tourism under a section of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which grants the president the power to set exceptions and limitations on who can enter into the country.On one of his first back days in office in 2025, Trump signed an executive order that tried to end birthright citizenship as guaranteed in the 14th Amendment to the US Constitution. A legal battle brought the case to the Supreme Court, which in June ruled that Trump's 2025 policies could not stand and birthright citizenship remained the law. The decision was a major blow to Trump's ongoing efforts to limit who can live, work, and become citizens in the US.The high court made "a bad decision, very unfair decision", Trump said from the Oval Office on Thursday while announcing the executive orders. "Our country suffers because of it, and we're ending in a different way."Gabriel Chin, a professor at the University of California Davis' School of Law, told the BBC that while parts of the order might hold up, other aspects "raise some serious constitutional questions".Chin said the president does have some power to restrict people coming into the US specifically for the purposes of having a child. "But once it does happen, once a child is born in the United States, I don't think the president has any power to decide that that child is not a citizen," he said, adding that the issue was settled in the Trump administration's recent loss in the Supreme Court. He called birth tourism a "drop in the bucket" against the millions of births in the US. "It's an unusual phenomenon," he said.

schema.headline: Trump again limits US birthright citizenship with new executive orders

title: Thailand school shooting: Pupil describes harrowing moment teacher was shot in front of her
description: I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil saysFigure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heardByJonathan Head
body: I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil saysFigure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heardByJonathan Head and Thanyarat DoksoneReporting fromDebsirin School, Nonthaburi and Tiffanie TurnbullOn Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok.Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire."I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot," a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up."Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room.Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured 23 people - including fellow pupils - before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents."I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends," the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues.Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'."Follow live: Thai teenager kills at least seven and injures more than 30 as PM calls shooting 'well prepared'Image source, ReutersImage caption, One student recounts having to climb over a fence to escapeOne 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought firecrackers were going off."I didn't think it was a gun at first," he said. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."Metres from the school gates, paramedics loaded the wounded into ambulances and rushed them to hospital, as milling crowds hugged and cried.Rescue worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith rushed to the scene after hearing children as young as 12 had been hurt."I saw students who had been shot, some in the arm, some in the back, some in the chest. So I rushed to help get them to the hospital first," the 47-year-old rescue worker told Reuters news agency.One grieving teacher told the BBC his friend was among the dead."She was my age. We went to this school together as students. Then we both became teachers at this school," the 31-year-old, who declined to give his name, said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Authorities say the 14-year-old shot five teachers dead, and more than 30 injuries have been reportedIt is early days in the investigation and police haven't said anything about a motive. They believe the 9mm handgun the shooter used belonged to his grandfather. Forensic officers found the gunman's shots to be "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies.Others are filling some of the gaps. A teacher at the school has said the shooter was a good student - not aggressive and with good grades - and education authorities have described him as an avid gamer.Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said study pressures may have played a role. "We learned that his grandmother was a teacher and she might have been strict with him. From what the police gathered from his close friend, they knew he was quite stressed about it."It is clear authorities will have many questions to answer in the coming days - many of them about what change this crime must trigger.Renewed calls for gun control reformThis is Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in years - and the second at a school this year.In February, a head teacher and a female student were shot by an 18-year-old gunman during a school siege in southern Thailand.Four years ago, a 34-year-old in the eastern Nong Bua Lamphu province killed 37 people, most of them preschoolers, in a shooting and stabbing at a nursery.These crimes have resurfaced questions about gun control in the country."This shouldn't have happened," the boyfriend of one of the killed teachers told reporters, clearly distressed and trying to hold back tears.More than seven million people are believed to own guns in the country, one of the highest rates of ownership in the world. Of those, more than one million are unlicensed owners.Image source, EPAImage caption, The shooting at Debsirin Nonthaburi School is the second in Thailand this yearWhile there are restrictions on gun licences in Thailand, people can still acquire the weapons - legally or illegally - with relative ease. There is a thriving black market, aided by Thailand's porous land borders with four other nations. Problems with corruption and loose regulation in the police and military have seen weapons end up in the wrong hands. Prime Minister Anutin said he had tightened regulations when he was interior minister three years ago - suspending new gun permits. But gun crime remains rife, with deaths from gunshots among the highest in the region. And some in the community are calling for greater action."An act of violence in an educational institution, which should be one of the safest places in our society, serves as a stark reminder for Thai society to seriously and systematically review gun control measures," Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the People's Party - an opposition party - wrote in a Facebook post.

schema.headline: Thailand school shooting: Pupil describes harrowing moment teacher was shot in front of her

title: Leipzig airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?
description: A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fir
body: A previous Russian-backed plot involving Leipzig airport could provide clues.In 2024, a parcel containing a sophisticated incendiary device caught fire at the airport's DHL hub shortly before it was loaded onto a plane. Similar packages then ignited in the UK and Poland, causing extensive damage.A group of men are currently on trial in both Lithuania and Poland, where prosecutors believe they were part of a substantial network of proxies recruited by Russian military intelligence.But there was a subplot that has been little discussed before.Last September, Lithuanian prosecutors said that investigators had also seized RDX explosives meant for "other terrorist attacks". The amount was significant: equivalent to 6kg of TNT."Some of the devices were manufactured to intensify the blast," the prosecutor added.The BBC has since had access to case documents that describe how several of the men on trial were paid to transport those explosives around Europe, concealed in cans of sweetcorn and chopped tomatoes. The detonators were hidden inside headphone sets.The suspects also handled drone parts and the case talks specifically of attachments, suitable for holding a bomb.Prosecutors allege that some of the items were brought into the EU from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.Almost two dozen suspects have been charged with terror offences, but with the men's handlers still at large, believed to be in Russia, it is not clear whether the entire network was disbanded or all the hidden material found.While there is no evidence of a link to the Leipzig drone bomb, the 2024 plot certainly highlights the potential.One of the suspects charged in Poland, a Ukrainian called Vladyslav D., described in detail to investigators how he made multiple long car trips in July 2024 following instructions from someone he knew as "Warrior".He has since pleaded not guilty in court.One message sent him to the edge of a Lithuanian forest where he found a carrier bag containing "three or four packs of headphones", soggy with rain.He had already collected two cans of corn "lightly covered with soil" from another location, telling investigators he had no idea what was inside.He was ordered to leave the headphones many hours' drive away in Poland where he noticed "a guy on a bicycle" collect them from beside the road.For another assignment he received a pin for a location inside a Lithuanian cemetery and was told to dig beneath some plastic flowers. He quickly uncovered a bin bag wrapped in brown tape."Inside were drone components: small plastic propellers, I think four pieces," Vladyslav told investigators.These items were to be left by a road in central Poland for pick-up.Finally there was a trip to Germany where he was given the code to access a hostel room in Dusseldorf. He was instructed to leave the drones and other items inside.The intended targets were never revealed.In statements to investigators, Vladyslav D. said he was paid more than $2,000 (£1,487) in cryptocurrency for his efforts. His motive was clear.And what about the Leipzig case?Few details about the drone bomb are yet public.Some German sources report that the explosive was Semtex, which contains RDX - the explosive found in the food cans in a Lithuanian cemetery.We do not know how much the drone found at the airport was carrying and the physical damage may have been limited."The drone casing, if it was metal, might have put a hole in the plane but just a blast wave probably would just have dented it unless they put some fragmentation inside," explosives expert Professor Jackie Akhavan of Cranfield University explained.But if Russia was behind this, its aim was more likely to sow fear.Andrei Soldatov, an expert on Russia's intelligence agencies, said it "makes sense" to suspect Moscow, pointing to a clear pattern of sabotage and hostile activity, from arson attacks on facilities supporting Ukraine to drones over sensitive sites in Europe.Germany is one of Kyiv's biggest suppliers of military aid."It's a message. You get something like that [bomb] into one of the biggest European airports and you send the message that, 'Guys, we can do that. Remember'," Soldatov explained."You hint to the adversary that you might cause a really big problem: that tomorrow might be more serious."And the potential motive? Moscow is under intense pressure from Ukraine's long-scale drone attacks, he said, and the fact that Russian President Vladimir Putin "has been humiliated, repeatedly"."We are aware of the incident, which the German authorities continue to investigate," a Nato official told the BBC.Antonov Airlines has also been cautious so far in its response.The firm supplies planes for certain Nato operations but declined to say whether that includes military support for Ukraine.Asked whether the Ukrainian planes might have been targeted, a spokeswoman in Kyiv told the BBC: "We are not making any such assumptions…We don't know what this drone was or why it was there."But Russia watchers are clear."This is Russian interference," said John Lough of the New Eurasian Strategies (NEST) Centre. "It's all part of undermining support for Ukraine by pointing to the dangers of escalation and, frankly, scaring the German authorities."He sees high potential for a surge in such hybrid attacks now because Ukraine has "changed the balance" of the war."My expectation is that such activity will increase quite sharply over the coming months. I think it's a dangerous moment."

schema.headline: Leipzig airport drone-bomb: Could Russia be involved?

title: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band Cortis weighs in on concert etiquette
description: Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-
body: Kicking off their global tour in the South Korean city of Incheon, the five members of K-pop boy band Cortis saunter onto stage in casual, streetwear-inspired outfits, exuding an effortlessly cool vibe."Put your phone down," one of the members bellows. Piercing screams erupt. A sea of illuminated screens flickers back."I told you, put your phone down," he repeats, louder this time.Some fans do just that, but the packed stadium vibrates harder with cheers as thousands of phones stay in the air.It's hard to say how serious this theatrical command is."Put your phone down" is also the name of Cortis's ongoing concert tour, which started in Incheon on 18 July and will head to cities like New York and Los Angeles before returning to Seoul later this month.The refrain reflects a message the band has long pushed: that fans should stop watching concerts through six-inch screens and engage with their performances in real life.It's drawn mixed reactions from their fandom: fan-filmed content is a valuable social currency in K-pop.Park Ji-yeon, for one, could not bring herself to stop recording Cortis's performances. The 22-year-old had specially rented a new, top-tier smartphone for both days of the Cortis concert just so she could film in the highest quality."I was standing right at the front, and I couldn't bring myself to put my phone down because I don't know if I'll ever get this opportunity again," she tells the BBC."I usually film concerts because I know a lot of those memories will fade as soon as I leave the venue."While fans like Park continued to film, some heeded the band's call. Kim Ga-eun, 25, who was seated in the amphitheatre-style venue, saw it all."People in the back of the standing section were having a great time dancing together. I thought that really reflected the intention behind the concert," she says.Cortis has had a whirlwind year since debuting last year under record label BigHit Music - part of the company that created pop sensation BTS. Most of its members are teenagers. The oldest of the group, James, is just 20 years old.Their music videos have each amassed millions of views. Over the weekend they performed at Lollapalooza, the famed music festival in Chicago.The band's name, Cortis, is derived from the phrase "colour outside the lines", which according to their record label is meant to encapsulate the band's free spirit and refusal to conform to societal rules - which, in this case, appears to include telling fans to resist the temptation of the phone camera.They join a prominent wave of artists around the world who have been advocating the same.Singers like Phoebe Bridgers and Alicia Keys have required their concert attendees to use lock pouches - sealed bags that allow people to hold on to their phones without being able to access them.Few have gone as far as British rock group Suede, whose frontman Brett Anderson leapt over a barricade during a 2023 performance in Singapore to grab at fans' phones.Billie Eilish, who has defended filming as a way for fans to relive precious memories after a show, gently cooed to her front row audience during a performance in Amsterdam: "Put your phone down, I'm right here."Even BTS, K-pop's golden boys, have made similar requests. "Stop looking at your phone screen. Just look at me," BTS member Jungkook teased the audience at one concert."From the artists' perspective, interacting with fans is a really important part of performing, so I think they want people to focus more on that than on their phones," Park says of Cortis's anti-mobile rallying cry.After all, fancams - zoomed-in videos focusing on a single celebrity - are a prized currency in K-pop communities. Once shared online, people meticulously study the choreography in them and delight in catching subtle movements and expressions by their favourite band members. These clips live on as fodder for collective swooning and fan-made montages.And this is why Cortis's incessant calls to for people to put their phones down have rubbed some the wrong way - in a fan culture that's obsessed with capturing every moment. After the first day of their concert, disgruntled comments emerged online among fans."I spent over one million won ($700; £520) attending both days," Park says, referring to the sum of not just concert tickets but also additional expenses like transport and accommodation."I think a lot of fans spent similar amounts of money, so constantly hearing them asking us to put our phones down made some fans even more frustrated."These murmurs appear to have reached Cortis, who fans say dialled down their message on the second day of the concert."On the first day, the message felt more like, 'Let's put our phones down and have fun together.' On the second day, it changed slightly to, 'We understand why you want to film, so let's just make sure we enjoy ourselves together,'" Kim recalls."They said filming was okay, but they wanted us to enjoy the concert together, and that 'Put Your Phone Down' was more of a mindset."

schema.headline: 'Put your phone down': K-pop band Cortis weighs in on concert etiquette

title: Thousands of migrants still in Ceuta after border crisis, local leader says
description: Figure caption, Watch: Migrants started to return to Morocco after thousands entered Spain's Ceuta on 30 JulyByAleks PhillipsBetween 3,000 and 5,000 m
body: Figure caption, Watch: Migrants started to return to Morocco after thousands entered Spain's Ceuta on 30 JulyByAleks PhillipsBetween 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in the Spanish territory of Ceuta following the arrival of many times that number of people last week, the north African exclave's leader has said.Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament of his "profound sorrow" over the "irreparable tragedy" of 100 deaths that had occurred after roughly 78,000 migrants from neighbouring Morocco arrived by sea in a matter of hours.His comments come as new calls for mass crossings circulate on social media, according to Moroccan media.The crisis has created tensions among EU nations who share open borders and has sparked criticism of the Spanish government.However the EU Commission has commended Spain's "swift response" to the crisis, which has included deploying armed forces to Ceuta and its other territory on the north African coast, Melilla.Vivas, a conservative, was critical of the national government's response while addressing the European Parliament on Thursday, saying that he had personally told Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez that it had been late and insufficient."The fact that we don't have numbers on how many are still in Ceuta shows how few resources we have to deal with this situation," Ceuta's mayor-president said. Previous warnings by local officials of an increase in migrant crossings by sea had been ignored, he said.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Thousands of migrant children are thought to remain in Ceuta, where they are being registered by the authoritiesVivas said that while the return of nearly 75,000 migrants to Morocco had "considerably alleviated" the situation, Ceuta had not yet returned to normal.There was still a humanitarian emergency and disturbances to public order in the territory, he said, while it was "basically impossible" to return the minors who had crossed because this required their consent.Spain's interior minister has said the government had allocated €25m (£21.4m; $28.8m) to assist minors in Ceuta.However, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reports that 4,860 migrant children have been registered by volunteer groups in Ceuta - double official estimates."Neighbours are taking them into their homes, but the situation is unsustainable," a volunteer told the paper.So far no migrant children have been moved to mainland Spain, with right-wing local authorities reluctant to take them in, according to El País.While some on the right have pointed to an agreement with Morocco stipulating co-operation on returning migrant children to their families, Melilla's conservative leader has called for a "gesture of solidarity" from his mainland colleagues.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Juan Jesús Vivas accused the Spanish government of ignoring the warning signs before the mass influx of migrantsIt is unclear exactly why tens of thousands of migrants attempted to cross into Ceuta on Thursday and Friday last week. The EU's Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner has suggested criminal networks spreading disinformation were to blame - an assertion Sánchez has agreed with.The crossings came after Spain's Supreme Court ruled that migrants stopped at sea while trying to reach Ceuta or Melilla cannot be summarily returned to Morocco.The two exclaves have long been a bone of diplomatic contention between Spain and Morocco, which does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over them.The number of people swimming to Ceuta at once has raised questions about why Morocco's border guards did not attempt to stop them. Vivas characterised the incident as an "unequivocal attack"."Our people feel sad, helpless, anxious, fearful and worried - and they have good reason to, because it is inevitable to wonder whether this will happen again," he commented.Spain's interior minister has said he was working "firmly" with Morocco to avoid further "violations", and that any migrants still in Ceuta would be returned there as soon as possible.Brunner said the EU should use all the leverage at its disposal, including visa policy and trade, to secure co-operation from Morocco on migration.Morocco, for its part, has laid blame for the crisis on Spain's Supreme Court, with an unnamed government source briefing local outlets that "the deterrent element of the system collapsed and the dam gave way, not under the weight of the criminals, but of a judge's decision".Meanwhile, Moroccan media is reporting fresh online calls to co-ordinate another mass border-crossing attempt, similar to what was seen before the influx last week.News site Hespress reports that posts and messages were circulating on social media to join closed WhatsApp groups, along with hashtags linked to migration to Spain and work opportunities there - despite warnings from Moroccan authorities that people promoting irregular migration could face prosecution.The Ceuta crossings have also caused a diplomatic rift among EU nations that share open borders as part of the Schengen area. Italy suspended its Schengen arrangement with Spain, backed by Finland and Denmark, while the Czech Republic called for Spain's membership to be temporarily suspended - despite Sánchez noting Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area.Brunner said the EU was "ready to do more" in Ceuta but had not received a further request for EU border guards from the Spanish government.

schema.headline: Thousands of migrants still in Ceuta after border crisis, local leader says

title: What is birthright citizenship and how common is birth tourism in the US?
description: Trump signed two executive orders, a written order issued by a president to the federal government which does not require congressional approval, on T
body: Trump signed two executive orders, a written order issued by a president to the federal government which does not require congressional approval, on Thursday.One expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.It prevents the automatic citizenship of babies born in the US to two non-citizen parents if one of the parents is a member of a foreign terrorist group, is a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not granted by US federal law. A few of those categories were already excluded under current birthright citizenship rules, but the one relating to membership of a foreign terrorist group could raise issues, according to Colleen Putzel-Kavanaugh, an associate policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, an independent nonpartisan research group.She said it is difficult to know how, when, and by whom membership would be determined, and it is also not clear "if the onus for proof falls on the government (to prove they are a member) or the individual (to prove they are not)".The second order, meanwhile, seeks to end the practice of birth tourism by directing the departments of state and homeland security to enhance regulations and expand enforcement against the practice. It is already illegal to travel to the US for the purpose of giving birth.According to the executive order, operators in the birth tourism industry use deceptive advertising to entice foreign nationals to give birth in the US. "They promise citizenship; access to public benefits; and short-term stays in specialised facilities, hotels, or rentals, but often fail to deliver on these promises," the order says. The principle of birthright citizenship, known in legal terms as "jus soli" or "right of the soil", is enshrined in the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution.The law was originally meant to grant citizenship to American-born, formerly enslaved people following the American Civil War.Currently, nearly everyone born in the US, regardless of their parents' citizenship status, is granted US citizenship - with a few exceptions. These include children born in the US to foreign diplomats, those born to enemy soldiers during a hostile occupation of US territory, and those born in unincorporated US territories where a federal statute has not granted the right to citizenship. People born in the US territories of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the US Virgin Islands, for example, get automatic citizenship, while those born in unincorporated American Samoa are not and are instead considered "non-citizen nationals".Trump said on Thursday that "hundreds of thousands" of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US, without providing evidence or clarifying if that figure is annual or not. There are no government figures specifically on women coming to the US on tourism visas to give birth, but there is data on foreign residents giving birth in the country.These show that just over 9,500 babies were born to foreign women in the US in 2024, according to the most recent estimate, external from the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). This is based on births registered to mothers with foreign addresses. In comparison, there were 3.7 million US births in total that same year, CDC figures show,, external meaning babies born to foreign US residents amounted to roughly 0.25% of these.However, the MPI says the government figures are likely an undercount and that foreigners could use a US address that is not their permanent home to register a birth.The MPI estimates, external that between 20,000 to 26,000 babies were born in the US annually as a result of birth tourism, which is about 0.5 to 0.7% of total annual births.This figure is based on a wider review of US census data, although their study notes that it is hard to know exact numbers for certain."Birth tourism inherently relies on the intent of an individual to come to the US to give birth and capturing that intent in data is difficult," said Putzel-Kavanaugh."For some women, they may be travelling and a medical emergency could necessitate birth in the US even if their intent was to give birth back in their home country."

schema.headline: What is birthright citizenship and how common is birth tourism in the US?

title: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity
description: Warning: This story contains details some may find distressingA 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belie
body: Warning: This story contains details some may find distressingA 17-year-old Sudanese girl holds a young child in her arms with a heavy calm that belies her age and the concerns she has for his future."This son of mine has no father, no birth certificate and no national number," Amira, whose name has been changed to protect her identity, tells the BBC.Looking down at him, she speaks slowly as if still trying to grasp the details of what has happened to her since the civil war erupted in Sudan.She and her family used to live in the eastern neighbourhoods of el-Fasher, a city that came under siege from the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in a brutal power struggle with the military since April 2023.El-Fasher was the army's last stronghold in the western region of Darfur until it fell to the RSF and allied Arab militias after 18 months last October.For the tens of thousands of civilians trapped inside the city, it was a nightmare – with constant bombardment, clashes and suffering from a lack of food.In the end Amira and her family decided to flee early in 2025, desperate to find a safer area.But as they snuck out on a road south-west of the city, she says she was abducted by three armed men from the RSF and held captive."They blindfolded me and took me to the Tabit area south of el-Fasher. I was locked in a room for two months, and every day one of them raped me in turn," she recounts in a low voiceAfter weeks in captivity, she discovered she was pregnant and became very sick.Amira says when the men wanted to get rid of her, they dropped her near the area she had been captured.It was with the help of other people fleeing el-Fasher that she was taken to receive medical help.Months later, at a humanitarian hub that was not under RSF control, she gave birth at a hospital run by the International Medical Corps.There she received some support from a Sudanese aid organisation - the Nada Al-Azhar Foundation for Disaster Prevention and Sustainable Development (Nada).The group was also able to find her family, who had made it to a camp where hundreds of thousands of people from el-Fasher have sought refuge.It was a huge relief for them all to be reunited, but the family still face challenges - one being that eight months after giving birth, Amira has been unable to register her son's birth."Even getting a birth notification from the hospital requires information that doesn't exist," says Amira, explaining that she is unable to provide any details about the child's father.Without this she cannot organise any official recognition of the baby's legal identity."I can't get him vaccinated, or enrol him in nursery or school," she says."I'm afraid for his future because he isn't registered at all. My economic situation is very difficult, and I can't afford his treatment or care. I can't even go to work for fear of being exposed to violence again."According to Nada, Amira's story is not an isolated case, but part of a reality repeated in areas experiencing conflict across Sudan.This is because many children are being born in complex circumstances, often without the knowledge of the father - meaning their births cannot be registered, explains Abu Bakr Yousif Yaqoub, Nada's director of protection programmes."Registering a child requires identity information, a national number and a birth certificate. But when the father is absent or unknown, it becomes extremely difficult," he tells the BBC from el-Fasher."The mother is often alone, and sometimes she herself is still a child who needs care, which limits her ability to care for her baby."There are also health challenges related to the lack of follow-up on essential vaccinations, which begin at birth and continue through the child's early years."He warns that this situation does not just affect a child's early years but extends to their future education and as an adult being able to travel or obtain official documents.It is not easy to obtain data about the number of children that have been born as a result of rape in Sudan.According to Nada's director general, Shaza Ahmed, this comes down to social stigma as the true numbers are not recorded."Women who experience such assaults do not feel comfortable reporting them," she tells the BBC, speaking from Port Sudan, an army-held city in the east of Sudan."Unfortunately, most of the mothers of these children are themselves children - girls under the age of 18. Therefore, they cannot make the decision to go officially to court or the police, as they need a guardian to accompany them."She notes that 90% of the cases recorded by her organisation involve families refusing to allow official reporting of the sexual assaults that led to pregnancy."As a Sudanese woman, my greatest fear and concern for children born as a result of rape is that we are facing a whole generation that will live under stigma, danger and fear," Ahmed says."These children will not receive respect from society, their well-being will not be truly protected, and above all, they will not have access to services or their rights."For Ahmed they are not being treated as if they are "fully human", even though Sudanese law does grant all children the right to obtain an identity.Sudanese lawyer Majida Idris explains that the Child Act of 2010 allows for the registration of children born outside marriage.But it relies on the mother being willing to file a report that she has been assaulted - because this kick starts the registration process.Once reported, the case is then referred to social services for documentation, before being sent to the civil registry, where the child is registered under the mother's name and given a full legal name according to procedures.However, Idris says that the reality during war is completely different, especially in Darfur, where the ongoing conflict has led to the collapse of civil services and the shutdown of civil registry offices, leaving thousands of children unregistered."The absence of documents does not just mean the absence of a piece of paper - it means denying the child access to education, healthcare and legal recognition," she tells the BBC.The lawyer says it is imperative to reactivate civil registry offices in accessible areas and intensify legal efforts to ensure children obtain their right to identity and legal recognition.Amira and her child remain in Darfur - and therefore in administrative limbo.Her mother admits that the lack of paperwork for her grandson is a worry.Yet for the moment the family is overwhelmed with gratitude to have found one another again.Amira has also been offered emotional and psychological support sessions and other advice by Nada - which is a comfort to the family."I was so extremely worried until I found her. I hadn't been eating or drinking," Amira's mother told the BBC."The reunion was like a miracle from God. To see our daughter back sitting among us is a gift and blessing that could not be thanked enough for."

schema.headline: Sudan's invisible children - born in war with no legal identity

title: Supreme Court on walking: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimatesByIndia correspon
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimatesByIndia correspondentFor much of my life, walking in Indian cities has felt less like exercising a right than negotiating an obstacle course.I grew up in Kolkata, where wide pavements disappeared beneath rows of hawkers. I moved to Delhi, where roads seemed designed almost exclusively for cars. Now I live in Gurugram, where footpaths vanish into rubble and garbage, are abruptly blocked by parked vehicles or construction, or sit uncomfortably high above the road.So when India's Supreme Court declared in June that the right to walk safely on designated footpaths was a fundamental right, external, it felt less like judicial activism than common sense arriving decades late.Walking is the most democratic form of transport. Yet it is also the one India's cities have neglected most consistently.It's remarkable because India remains, above all, a nation of walkers. Around 45 million people walk to work every day, according to census-based estimates, compared with only about 5.4 million who commute in private cars, jeeps or vans.Nearly a third of urban workers walk to work, while virtually every bus or metro journey begins and ends on foot. Add school runs, shopping trips and other everyday journeys, and walking dominates urban mobility. A 2019 survey of selected cities found that 63% of all journeys were made on foot, making pedestrians the single largest group of road users.Many are what researchers call "captive pedestrians" - people who walk not by choice but because they cannot afford another option. Women are especially dependent on walking. Yet the people who contribute least to congestion and pollution often face the greatest risks.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman walks past poles and wires strewn across a footpath in ChennaiThe evidence is harrowing. Even where pavements exist, they are often broken, narrow or inaccessible to older people, children and those with disabilities.They are also blocked by motorcycles, swallowed by parked cars, encroachments or excavated for utility works. Faded zebra crossings are treated as little more than road markings no-one respects. Flyovers speed traffic while forcing pedestrians into hazardous detours below. A landmark 2011 study of six Indian cities found that India's streets routinely fail pedestrians because of "poor and unsafe" infrastructure.The Walkability in Indian Cities report by the Clean Air Initiative for Asian Cities (CAI-Asia) gave the surveyed cities a median walkability score of just 47 out of 100, with the worst conditions around public transport terminals - ironically the places where most journeys begin and end on footAs Geetam Tiwari, a transport scholar at Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi puts it, pedestrians have been "pushed to the margins of the road networks" forcing them to "jostle for space with motor vehicles".The price is paid in lives.Officially pedestrians account for roughly a fifth of road deaths, external, but independent studies cited by Tiwari estimate the share is closer to 30-40%.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Motorcyclists riding on a pedestrian footpath along a bridge in DelhiPedestrians are also the second-largest group of road accident victims after two-wheeler riders. In Delhi and Mumbai, they account for more than half of all road deaths. According to a World Bank study, crashes already cost India an estimated 3-5% of its GDP each year through lost productivity, healthcare costs and disability.The Supreme Court case arose from one such tragedy: a five-year-old boy crushed by a truck while walking to school with his father.The judges responded with unusual eloquence. Walking, Justice PS Narasimha wrote, is "the simplest of the simple human activity, inextricably connected to life". Roads therefore impose a corresponding duty on the state to provide safe footpaths. "The fundamental right to walk on demarcated footpaths shall override the privilege of a motorised vehicle," he declared.The judgment challenges decades of Indian urban planning, where progress has often been measured in kilometres of expressways, flyovers and elevated corridors. Streets were engineered to move vehicles as quickly as possible, while the one road user every citizen inevitably becomes - the pedestrian - largely disappeared from planners' imagination."People know about the latest cars, but walking has become invisible," says Rishi Aggarwal, who has spent more than a decade trying to change that mindset in Mumbai.Through city walks and public talks, his advocacy group, Walking Project, encourages residents to notice what they have stopped seeing: broken pavements, blocked crossings and unsafe junctions - and compare them with the standards pedestrians are entitled to expect. "When people become apathetic, they stop observing the street," he says.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Zebra crossings - like this one in Kolkata - are treated as little more than road markings In a city where an estimated 15 million walking trips are made every day, Aggarwal argues, it is not just footpaths that have disappeared from view, but also the millions of people who depend on them.For Rahul Goel, a transportation researcher at Delhi's Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), the problem begins with governance. "Are footpaths maintained and cleaned? Does the city ensure they aren't encroached upon?" he says. "In Delhi, many roads do have footpaths, but they're often unusable because of poor governance."Poor design makes matters worse. Cars parked perpendicular to the kerb often conceal footpaths or block them altogether, while vehicles parked directly on pavements are a common sight. Footpaths are often too narrow for the number of pedestrians. Many are so high above the road that older people, wheelchair users and others with limited mobility struggle to use them. Others end abruptly, forcing people back onto the carriageway."If the footpath is discontinuous, it's simply more convenient to keep walking on the road," says Goel.He believes the deeper problem is one of priorities. "Urban transport governance is still centred on moving vehicles. Reducing congestion and maximising road space for motor traffic take precedence over pedestrians," he says. Civic agencies are often reluctant to widen footpaths because they view carriageway space as sacrosanct. That mindset, Goel argues, is reinforced by public pressure. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, A pedestrian walks through a haze of dust pollution in HyderabadTraffic jams dominate headlines and social media, pushing authorities to keep vehicles moving. In Delhi, many mid-block crossings have been replaced by U-turns to reduce stoppages, forcing pedestrians onto foot overbridges. "People don't just need to walk along a road," says Goel. "They need to be able to cross it safely too."The result is a stark urban inequality. In Gurugram, a high-speed arterial road cuts through busy neighbourhoods with few safe crossings. Domestic workers, labourers and other pedestrians routinely dodge speeding traffic, and many are killed trying to cross. Only after the death toll mounted did authorities begin building footbridges.Across India's cities, those who cannot afford cars or motorcycles are left to risk their lives on roads that barely accommodate pedestrians. Those who can drive claim an ever-larger share of public space, while walking becomes a leisure activity confined to gated communities, parks or gym treadmills. In a country grappling with rising obesity and lifestyle diseases, cities have turned the most basic form of exercise into something not just inconvenient, but too often dangerous.Clearly, making people walk will require far more than a court order."Walking as a fundamental right should lead to pedestrian-friendly cities, not just pedestrian-friendly streets," says Tiwari.That means rethinking how cities are designed. Some countries have adopted default urban speed limits of 30km/h or 20mph to protect pedestrians, regardless of the type of road. Achieving that, Tiwari says, requires redesigning streets by narrowing traffic lanes, altering road surfaces and introducing other traffic-calming measures. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, A man with a physical disability navigates a busy road in KolkataThe judges also reflected on walking as something far greater than a way of getting from one place to another. It can be "necessity for the poor, meditation for some, an act of resistance for others and a path to discovery. Walking, they noted, also helped shape India's freedom struggle".As writer Sumana Roy notes, external, India's political history has often unfolded on foot -from Gandhi's "salt march" to Dandi to Subhas Chandra Bose's "Delhi Chalo" (March to Delhi) and the many protest marches that followed.For Tiwari, that broader understanding of walking should also shape how cities are built. "Walking is more than a travel option," she says. "Therefore a safe walking infrastructure requires more than creating footpaths and safe crossing. Walking spaces have to integrate activities like spaces of street vendors, shaded paths, areas for resting for old people and sometimes space where children can play."For decades, Indian cities have asked how to move more vehicles. The top court has reminded them to ask a simpler one: how do people walk?I'd settle for something wonderfully unremarkable: a footpath that simply carries me from one end of the street to the other.

schema.headline: Supreme Court on walking: India is a nation of walkers - but its cities forgot them

title: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
description: Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, The Afghan women's football team gathered for the first time since Fifa ruled they could represen
body: Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, The Afghan women's football team gathered for the first time since Fifa ruled they could represent their country in official matchesByMahjooba NowrouziBBC News Afghan LanguagesReporting fromAuckland, New ZealandThe changing room is busy with footballers going through their pre-match routines. Some stretch and tighten their boots, others embrace."Be strong as always because we are representing Afghan women," says midfielder Fatima Haidari to fellow members of Afghan Women United.Applause erupts in the room where an Afghan flag hangs and a patriotic song is played. As the women sing along some struggle to hold back tears.There's a final team huddle with words of encouragement from their coach before they head out to the pitch – a place that for years they had been told they did not belong.The 23-player squad, selected from Afghan players now living abroad, has travelled to New Zealand for a training camp and to play two unofficial friendly games against the Cook Islands.This is the first time they have been together since football governing body Fifa ruled in April that they could represent their country in official matches in the future.Image source, Afghan Women UnitedImage caption, The team hopes that in the future they will qualify for international competitions, such as the World Cup and the OlympicsPreviously, they would have needed the approval of the Afghanistan Football Federation. This was not possible under the Taliban, who returned to power in August 2021, imposing wide-ranging restrictions on women and girls, including barring them from secondary school and university, most professions and organised sport.The country's national women's team, formed in 2007, could no longer play and its members were among those evacuated and resettled in countries including Australia, the UK and Portugal.Years of campaigning led to the creation of a refugee team, which became Afghan Women United. Thanks to Fifa's ruling, it can now try to qualify for international competitions such as the Olympics and World Cup.Gathered in New Zealand, the squad is excited to be playing together - as asylum seekers living in various countries it has been hard for them to get the travel documents in order to train as a team over the past five years.Sitting in the hotel in Auckland the day before the match, Manozh Noori, who has short hair, wears a T-shirt and knee-length shorts - a look that she says has often drawn criticism from relatives for looking too masculine.As the 23-year-old speaks to BBC Global Women about her family, her voice begins to falter. She pauses, takes a deep breath and looks away for a moment before continuing. There are no tears, but the emotion is clear.Image caption, Manozh Noori buried her medals in her garden before she left AfghanistanNoori now lives in Australia but she grew up playing football with boys in the streets of Kabul.After seeing women's football on television, she secretly joined local clubs and gradually rose through the ranks in Afghanistan.She knew her older brother would disapprove so she tried to reduce the risk of being recognised by wearing a face covering.Over six years, she won league titles, national championships and individual awards.Eventually her success became impossible to hide. In about 2018 her fellow players persuaded her to remove her face covering for a TV interview, which was shown on the news along with highlights of their match.Then she had to face the reality that her brother might see it. "I was so scared," she recalls. "I kept thinking, 'He's going to see me. He's going to know.'"In desperation, she tried to stop the family from watching the news by turning off the electricity, but word soon reached her brother and he was furious, she says."He was screaming," Noori says. "'You told us you were studying. You said you wanted to become a teacher or a doctor. What is this?'"He threatened to cut his ties with the family if she didn't stop, she adds. "My mother was crying. She told me, 'He's the person who supports us financially. How are we going to survive?'"Image source, Manozh NooriImage caption, Noori (in blue) used to wear a face mask to hide her identity when playing in Afghanistan  Noori did stop playing for a while, but eventually started again. She says her other brother, who lives in Germany, sent money to help finance her dream.When the Taliban took over in 2021, Noori decided to flee, but first she buried her football medals and trophies in the garden of her family home.More than four years later, they remain there."One day I will go back and dig them out," she says, briefly smiling at the thought."Football helped me get my mum and sister out of Afghanistan," she says. Two years after she moved to Australia and established herself as a football player, she was able to bring them over as well.This meant her sister was able to study again - even though her brother didn't want them playing sports, he always supported their education.  "I hope my brother now realises I am not a bad person," says Noori.Afghan Reunited: The fight for footballBBC Global Women follows Afghan female footballers as they return to the pitchAs she and the team prepare for the matches in Auckland, many of them describe football as the reason they survived one of the most turbulent periods in their country's recent history."If I wasn't a footballer, I would still be in Afghanistan, one of millions of girls who are not allowed to study, speak up or choose their own future," says Mursal Sadat, who also lives in Australia.Now 24, she works as a football coach, youth facilitator and advocate for refugees, women's rights and human rights.Image caption, Mursal Sadat (kneeling right) was 19 when the Taliban returned to power - she was among those evacuated from Kabul in August 2021 In Afghanistan, she says she was often judged, harassed and told that no-one would want to marry a woman who played sport.Today she is engaged to a man who is still in Afghanistan, and says he and his family are supportive of her work and place on the national team. "They tell me, 'You are the pride of our family. We are so lucky to have you.'"As the players step out into the driving Auckland rain to face the Cook Islands, they channel their energy and determination, unfazed by the weather. They have faced much tougher conditions back home.As a teenager, defender Najma Arefi trained in temperatures above 45C (113F) because girls were often given the least desirable training slots.Still, she persisted.The 22-year-old's efforts eventually helped a Herat-based team win a national championship.The victory, she says, changed attitudes towards women's sport in the city."There were billboards of us across Herat," she recalls. "People were proud. More families started letting their daughters play football."She now lives in Doncaster in northern England. She arrived in the UK after the Taliban takeover.She describes herself as an extrovert and says she now has opportunities she never imagined growing up in Afghanistan.Image source, Phil Walter/Getty ImagesImage caption, Najma Arefi, pictured during one of the matches against the Cook Islands, moved to the UK after the Taliban returned to powerShe studies criminal justice at college, plays football and makes decisions independently. "Having that freedom is incredible," she says.Yet she admits she often feels guilty and desperately sad about the freedoms denied to women back home."Millions of girls don't have the chance to study or follow their dreams. I feel I have to make the most of every opportunity."Sometimes I put too much pressure on myself," she says, tears rolling down her face.She thanks Khalida Popal, who founded the original Afghan women's team, for pushing Fifa to recognise them now they are in exile.  "To receive Fifa's recognition without the approval of the Taliban" has made history, she says.This official status is "something I'll always be proud of", she says.When the BBC asked the Taliban's director for sports, Ahmadullah Wasiq, about Fifa backing the women's team, he declined to comment. But he said he would like Fifa to visit the country and resume its support for football there in general - the organisation largely withdrew after the Taliban came to power. Fifa has previously said any resumption of support would depend on women being allowed to play.The game in Auckland turns out to be unforgiving. A single goal in the first match hands the Cook Islands a 1-0 victory. Three days later, despite the Afghan team's best efforts, the Cook Islands win again, this time 3-0.Yet for the players, these matches represent something far more significant than two defeats.A return to the pitch and proof that despite exile, separation from their families and years of uncertainty, Afghanistan's women footballers refused to disappear.This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

schema.headline: Banned from football at home, Afghan women's team reunite 8,000 miles away
